clue.text: Victim of power-cut distressed ?

parts.note: read 'distressed' as de-tressed, shorn of his locks: the Biblical strongman lost his strength when Delilah had his hair cut

explanation.surface: Someone left upset by an electricity blackout.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power-cut' looks like a blackout, but it is a cutting that took away a man's power, and 'distressed' means having his tresses removed.
explanation.definitionFit: In Judges, the hero's strength lay in his uncut hair, so shaving it robbed him of his might.

clue.text: New-comer, say, didn't give a fig? On the contrary

definitions.text: didn't give a fig? On the contrary

indicators.note: New says the letters of the following words are made into something fresh

explanation.surface: A newcomer didn't care at all, or quite the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New-comer' looks like one word, but 'New' signals a rearrangement of COMER with SAY; 'didn't give a fig? On the contrary' means the tree did yield figs.
explanation.definitionFit: The Biblical sycomore is Ficus sycomorus, a fig tree that bears edible fruit.

clue.text: Writer to make one act heartlessly

parts.note: to marry is to make a couple one

indicators.note: heartlessly says the middle letter of the word act is removed

explanation.surface: An author sets out to unite with someone and acts cruelly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' drops the C from ACT, leaving AT.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Frederick Marryat was a Victorian novelist of sea stories.

clue.text: Red for the footballer's card? Well, no

definitions.meaning: a red card is shown to send a player off, so red is the shade for being dismissed

explanation.surface: A referee shows a red card, and someone questions whether that was right.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words: the colour of the card that sends a footballer from the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Red is the hue of the dismissal card; feeling unwell is being somewhat ill.

clue.text: Success of strikes

parts.note: to strike is to smash
to strike is also to hit

explanation.surface: A string of industrial strikes proving effective.
explanation.walkthrough: One word, 'strikes', supplies both halves: two different verbs for a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A big popular hit, a song or show that sells hugely, is a resounding success.

clue.text: 2's simple chap avoiding extremes, on board

definitions.note: the definition refers to the writer at 2-down: one of his novels

parts.note: a junior naval officer, whose title suggests a man in the middle of the vessel, away from bow and stern
easy means simple

explanation.surface: A naive fellow keeps to the middle of the deck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoiding extremes, on board' suggests amidships: the man in the middle of the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Midshipman Easy (1836) is Captain Marryat's best-known sea novel.

clue.text: To date redhead, get 'a couch, first

indicators.note: first puts the couch word before the head of red

parts.note: a sofa is a couch
the head of the word red is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone advises: before dating a redhead, buy a couch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'redhead' is one word but read as red's head, R; 'first' puts SOFA before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Up to now, until the present moment.

clue.text: Falconer's pet subjects

parts.note: a hobby is a small falcon, so a falconer's birds may be these, and pet subjects are pastimes

explanation.surface: The topics a falconer loves to talk about.
explanation.walkthrough: The hobby is a small falcon, so the falconer's birds and anyone's favourite pastimes share the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastimes are one's favourite pursuits, and a hobby is also a species of small falcon.

clue.text: Unnamed people grab gold held by speculators

indicators.note: grab says the people word takes hold of the gold word inside it

parts.note: they is the pronoun for unnamed people, as in 'they say'
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Anonymous figures seize the gold that investors were holding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by speculators' looks like the gold's owners; it defines an idea that thinkers hold.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypothesis is an idea proposed by thinkers who conjecture rather than prove.

clue.text: Fly for ever and ever in Australia

definitions.text: Fly for ever and ever in Australia

parts.words: Fly for ever and ever in Australia
parts.note: Peter Pan's island, reached by flying, where children never grow up, is also the Australian name for the remote outback

explanation.surface: A traveller flies on and on across Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter Pan flies to the island where no one ages; Australians use the same name for the far interior.
explanation.definitionFit: J M Barrie's fantasy island, where children stay young for ever, also names the Australian outback.

clue.text: Footsore runners' on the farm

parts.note: a corn is a painful patch on the foot, the thing that makes one footsore
the field is all the runners in a race

explanation.surface: Weary-footed racers out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a field of wheat is a place found on the farm.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheat or barley field is part of the land of a typical arable holding.

clue.text: Left edge of fairway, semi-playable lie

indicators.note: the left-hand edge of a written word is its first letter
semi means half, so only the second half of the word playable is kept

explanation.surface: A golfer's ball sits at the fringe of the fairway in a barely playable lie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie' poses as the golf sense, a ball's position; it is the definition as an untruth. 'semi-' keeps ABLE, the back half of 'playable', after F.
explanation.definitionFit: A tale such as Aesop's is an invented story, hence a falsehood or untruth.

clue.text: Centre for socialist day trippers

parts.note: the socialist day is May Day, 1 May, and the trippers are folk dancers circling a beribboned pole at the centre of the village green

explanation.surface: A destination for left-wing activists on an outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trippers' suggests excursionists, but here they trip the light fantastic; May Day is both the labour holiday and the old English spring festival.
explanation.definitionFit: On 1 May villagers traditionally dance round a tall ribboned post, so it stands at the heart of the festivities.

clue.text: Aircraft carrier — note bow replacement

indicators.note: the bow is the front of a vessel, so the opening letter of the word carrier is swapped for another

parts.note: H is a musical note in German notation, the B natural

explanation.surface: A naval vessel needs a new front section.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aircraft carrier' reads as one ship, but 'Aircraft' alone is the definition. 'bow replacement' swaps the C at the front of CARRIER for H.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hawker Siddeley jump jet, a vertical take-off warplane, bore this bird-of-prey name.

clue.text: Ten to three, say ? Nelson's lost half an hour

indicators.note: lost says some letters disappear from the admiral's name

parts.note: Admiral Nelson's first name was Horatio

indicators.note: half of the four-letter word hour is its first two letters

explanation.surface: Someone notes the time of ten to three, and Nelson is half an hour late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ten to three' looks like a clock time; it is a proportion, 10:3. 'lost' takes HO, the first half of 'hour', from HORATIO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten to three expresses a proportion between two quantities, which is exactly what such a relation is.

clue.text: It might put me in post improperly

definitions.text: It might put me in post improperly

indicators.note: improperly says the letters of these words are arranged wrongly

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone could be given a job unfairly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: favouritism to relatives is what could improperly put 'me' in a post.
explanation.definitionFit: Favouring one's relatives when appointing to jobs is the classic way someone gets a position unfairly.

clue.text: Cutty Sark's prize ending chapter of accidents

definitions.meaning: in Burns's poem Tam o' Shanter, the witch Cutty Sark grabs the tail of Tam's mare Meg as he escapes
an ornament printed at the end of a book's chapter, the chapter here a series of mishaps

explanation.surface: A tea clipper wins a prize that ends a run of misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: Cutty Sark suggests the clipper ship, but it is the witch in Burns's Tam o' Shanter, left holding the mare's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: The witch was left clutching the mare's rear appendage; a printer's decoration closes a chapter.

clue.text: Some misfire for me despite being improved

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone complains of a few failures despite getting better.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone mended in their ways has been made better or corrected.

clue.text: African capital by way of following US doctrine mostly

indicators.note: following puts the 'by way of' word after the doctrine's name
mostly means all but the last letter of the doctrine's name

parts.note: the Monroe Doctrine was the US policy opposing European meddling in the Americas
via means by way of

explanation.surface: Travelling to a capital city by way of American foreign policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' looks like 'adhering to' the doctrine, but it is the indicator that puts the 'by way of' word after the trimmed doctrine name.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Liberia, named after US President James Monroe.

clue.text: Minimize friction-it's. exploited after strike

definitions.meaning: to grease thoroughly, two words meaning lubricate fully
after striking oil, prospectors pump from the bore

explanation.surface: Someone urges calm in a dispute that is exploited after industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike' suggests industrial action; it is striking oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Lubricating thoroughly reduces rubbing; a drilled hole pumps crude once found.

clue.text: Like unpaid Pied Piper, that is as rat-catcher

indicators.note: catcher says the 'that is' letters hold the rodent within them

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The legend of the Pied Piper of Hamelin, whose fee went unpaid after he cleared the town of rats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rat-catcher' reads as a description of the Piper, but 'catcher' is the container signal: the abbreviation for 'that is' catches the rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheated of his fee, the Pied Piper was furious, enough to lure away the town's children.

clue.text: A card game which produces contract

parts.note: bridge is a card game

explanation.surface: A bridge game where a contract is bid.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge a contract is the bid declarer must make, but here it is a verb meaning shorten.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten a text is to condense or cut it down.

clue.text: Dagger mark ruins blouse

indicators.note: ruins says the letters of the garment word are wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: A knife stain spoils a shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dagger mark' suggests a stab; it is the printer's dagger sign, also called an obelisk.
explanation.definitionFit: The printer's dagger symbol, used for footnotes or to mark doubtful passages.

clue.text: Ball cut to boundary-hence his declaration ?

indicators.note: cut says the word Ball loses one of its letters

parts.note: a boundary in cricket scores four runs

explanation.surface: A cricketer cuts the ball to the boundary and then declares the innings closed.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a cut is a stroke and 'declaration' ends an innings, but here it is the 1917 British statement on Palestine, named after the Foreign Secretary.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur, Foreign Secretary in 1917, signed the letter backing a Jewish homeland in Palestine that bears his name.

clue.text: Sketch of ball on green in the open

parts.note: an outline drawing of a ball is a circle, the letter O
vert is green in heraldry

explanation.surface: A drawing of a golf ball on the putting green, out in the fresh air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' sets O on top of VERT in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Done openly, not concealed, is public and unhidden.

clue.text: Appears to store bits of this grass twice

annotationWithheld.why: Clue 'Appears to store bits of this grass twice (7)' as printed: the grass's letters form an anagram of 'pears to' within 'Appears to', but no reading accounts for 'store bits of this grass twice' or the spare A and P without words doing two jobs.
annotationWithheld.clue: Appears to store bits of this grass twice

clue.text: Lord's supporter holds one key

definitions.note: Lord's is read as 'Lord is', the 's joining definition to wordplay

indicators.note: holds says the supporter word has the 'one' letter put inside it

parts.note: a leg is a supporter, as of a table or a person
I is the Roman numeral for one
E is a musical key

explanation.surface: At Lord's cricket ground, a fielder in the leg position has one key.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's suggests the London cricket ground, but it is 'Lord is'.
explanation.definitionFit: In feudal times a vassal owed loyalty to his overlord, his sovereign master.

clue.text: City twice amended, so to speak

definitions.text: City twice amended, so to speak

parts.words: City twice amended, so to speak
parts.note: read 'amended' as am-ended, ended with the letters AM, and 'twice' as at both ends: the Dutch capital begins and ends with that pair

explanation.surface: A town whose charter has been revised on two occasions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so to speak' warns that 'amended' must be split into AM-ENDED; the city's name starts and finishes with AM.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch capital, a canal city in the Netherlands, has AM at both its beginning and end.

clue.text: You alone find it

parts.note: a state that only a person on their own can reach, since company destroys it

explanation.surface: A claim that only one person can discover something.
explanation.definitionFit: Being by oneself, away from company, is a condition reached only when alone.

clue.text: Note record finish, hang it -all

parts.note: D is a musical note
an EP is an extended-play record
end means finish

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated by a musical recording's ending cries 'hang it all!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'hang it all' reads as an oath, but 'hang' alone defines, as in 'hang on' or 'rely'; 'it all' completes the surface ('it all depends').
explanation.definitionFit: To hang on something is to rely or be contingent upon it.
